answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This line is confirmed: it is item 2, “Silence,” in the mock virtue-list Lawrence sets against Benjamin Franklin’s thirteen virtues in his essay collection Studies in Classic American Literature ↗ (1923).

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
Then for a ‘list.’ It is rather fun to play at Benjamin.
1. TEMPERANCE…
2. SILENCE. Be still when you have nothing to say; when genuine passion moves you, say what you’ve got to say, and say it hot.
3. ORDER…
trail: First published in the United States in August 1923 by Thomas Seltzer, per the Wikipedia entry on the book ↗.
The exact line appears verbatim in Chapter II, in the full text hosted by Project Gutenberg ↗.
An independent transcription at americanliterature.com ↗ carries the same wording in the same context.

author.heading: About D.H. Lawrence
author.bio: David Herbert Lawrence was an English novelist, poet, and critic best known for Sons and Lovers, The Rainbow, Women in Love, and the censorship-battling Lady Chatterley’s Lover. Alongside his fiction he wrote sharp, freewheeling literary criticism — including Studies in Classic American Literature, the source of this line.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In Studies in Classic American Literature, Lawrence devotes his Benjamin Franklin chapter to needling Franklin’s famous self-improvement program of thirteen virtues from the Autobiography. Rather than simply criticize the list, Lawrence writes his own counter-list — a looser, more instinctual set of maxims that answers Franklin virtue for virtue.

“Silence” is the second entry. Where Franklin’s original virtue counseled avoiding trifling conversation, Lawrence’s version turns it into something closer to a writer’s ethic: hold your tongue until you truly mean it, then speak with heat.
